records.text: Abstract

This paper gives a self-contained natural-language exposition of the expanded Wilson Yang–
Mills Construction: Mathematical Translation. For a given closed matrix subgroup of U(m) with
nonabelian simple real Lie algebra, the construction supplies one calibrated four-dimensional
Wilson family, full ﬁxed-period mesh limits and a subsequential outer volume limit, a common
hierarchy of local ﬁelds and phases, and a selected local Wightman theory with Poincaré covari-
ance, forward-cone spectrum and a unique vacuum. We give the ﬁnite quadratic kernels and
nonlinear geometry, marked integration, coupling reset and shooting histories, physical detec-
tor and equation quotient, phase and boundary reconstruction, separated and nested operator
products, contact extensions, and the ﬁnite-to-continuum stress and trace calculation with their
hypotheses and derivations. The centered trace obeys

lim
r↓0 r8 log2(1/r)GΘ(r) = 3 dimR g

The associated exclusions retain their stated ﬁnite mass-shell and Maxwell comparison hypothe-
ses. No positive mass gap is asserted. Two formula amendments are derived and documented
with the conventions used throughout the argument.

Attribution.
The underlying Yang–Mills Lean work is credited to OpenAI. Jeremy Rodgers
prepared this mathematical exposition with AI assistance.
Funding. No external funding.

1
Introduction: the construction and its dependencies

The starting point is a ﬁnite probability law: group elements live on oriented lattice links, and the
Wilson action measures each plaquette’s departure from the identity. The problem addressed by
the supplied construction is to control one family of these laws while the mesh tends to zero and the
physical period subsequently tends to inﬁnity. Inserting local gauge-invariant functions into that
same family is meant to produce a compatible hierarchy, rather than unrelated limits for diﬀerent
observables. The public theorem in Section 2 states the exact common-family and subsequence
quantiﬁers.
The derivation proceeds through a ﬁnite linear model, an actual nonlinear integration, and
two successive continuum limits. The quadratic model provides local inverse kernels and stationary
response maps. Nonlinear charts compare group links with that model, while positive energy bounds
pay for exceptional conﬁgurations. Marked local activities keep products of insertions attached to
the same represented density. An exact reset identity and ﬁnite coupling shooting select calibrated
histories on one calendar. Detector estimates then separate physical label classes and identify the
equation image before the common continuum hierarchy is formed. These constructions supply the
estimates and compatibility statements used in the limits and reconstruction.
Reﬂection positivity and slab bounds provide Hilbert-space control. The ground compression
algebra supplies the phase space and its measure; tube continuation and tempered boundary limits
supply ﬁelds on one common dense domain. The ﬁnal part returns to actual ﬁnite current and
stress functions. Their local equation estimates, coeﬃcient calibration and Gaussian comparison
determine a conserved physical stress and the centered trace. Positivity upgrades comparison along
arbitrary retained scaling sequences to the full positive-distance trace limit. That limit supports
the precise comparison exclusions stated in the public theorem.

Source and the two-paper release.
The mathematical source is the expanded project ex-
traction, Mathematical Translation [1], prepared with AI assistance. It presents the Yang–Mills
construction associated with the Lean work credited to OpenAI. This paper develops that source
as a complete mathematical exposition. Its deﬁnitions, hypotheses, estimates and derivations are
included here, together with the formula amendments in Appendix A.
The accompanying ﬂagship paper, Shadow Theory and the Wilson Yang–Mills Construction: A
Source–Readout Reconstruction [2], applies Jeremy Rodgers’s Shadow Theory, source–readout and
Source Lift programme to this construction [3]. Rodgers originated and directed that programme;
AI assisted its execution and the preparation of the two expositions. The papers share the Zenodo
release 10.5281/zenodo.24173681. Each contains its complete mathematical development: this pa-
per presents the construction, and the ﬂagship develops its source–readout realization and recovery.
Their common subject does not require a reader of either paper to obtain an essential derivation
from the other.
The given gauge group, faithful representation, four-dimensional lattice, Wilson action and
calibration conventions are physical and mathematical inputs. The detailed construction supplies
stress Ward identities, nested expansions and contact extensions on its common witnesses; the
public theorem retains its original list of clauses.

How to read the argument.
Read the ﬁnite setup and conventions ﬁrst, especially the healthy-
domain derivative and support budgets. The quadratic section explains the aliases, metric amend-
ment and ﬁlled stationary predictors. The nonlinear and marked-integration sections use those
objects to prove an actual density identity. The long scale-history section then buys every ﬁxed ﬁ-
nite request in a speciﬁed order, and distinguishes a full Cauchy limit from an auxiliary extraction.

The label, shell-charge and quotient sections are needed for reconstruction and stress detection.
The OPE, contact, Gaussian and trace sections retain their own ﬁnite horizons, comparison devices
and domains. The closing assembly returns to the theorem and identiﬁes all its witnesses on one
family and one reﬁnement.

Background.
The ﬁnite law is Wilson’s lattice formulation [4]; compact group integration uses
Haar measure [5]. Wick pairings [6], reﬂection positivity and Euclidean reconstruction [10, 11, 12],
chessboard inequalities [13], positive-functional representations [7, 8], and the character-algebra
approximation [9] form the mathematical background. Renormalization and cluster methods are
described in [16, 17, 18, 14]; the ﬁeld-theoretic framework is that of [15], and the conventional
one-loop coeﬃcient is associated with [19, 20]. These references credit the background; the actual
hypotheses, constants and derivations used here are stated locally.

The selected theory has a normalized vacuum Ωand one
common dense complex invariant domain, the span of ﬁnite smeared ﬁeld words applied to Ω.

vector depend continuously on the test. They satisfy the smeared adjoint identity, spacelike local

whose joint energy-momentum projection measure is supported in the closed forward cone. The

and at least one ﬁeld acts nontrivially. The public symmetry coordinates cover every proper or-
thochronous aﬃne Poincaré transformation. The selected Euclidean correlations are the values of
a holomorphic continuation in the tube of strictly ordered imaginary times. Its smeared boundary
limits on product Schwartz tests give the Wightman vacuum moments.

tori is required.

The order of choices in the spectral sign walk

We record the quantitative induction that supplies the small mixed-band bound in (RT6). Let Q
be the ﬁnite set of axes being tested, with two signs assigned so that each axis has an opposite-sign
partner. Let U ⊆Q be the axes whose width exponent is still allowed to be negative, and let i be

The common witnesses assembled here establish the public theorem’s quantiﬁers. All degree hori-
zons, derivatives, label coordinates, operator products and trace comparisons are consumed on one
Wilson family and one composite reﬁnement. The inner mesh limit remains full at every suitable
period; only the outer volume limit is subsequential. The detailed construction supplies additional
stress and contact information on these common witnesses without changing the list of clauses in
the public theorem.

We assemble the choices to verify the quantiﬁers of the theorem.
Fix the given group and
representation. Choose blocking penalty 1. The linear kernel construction gives its positive widths
and stagewise lower bounds on block ratios. The nonlinear geometry, Gaussian and connected-
activity estimates give further stagewise bounds, with block ratio chosen ﬁrst, then the remaining
ﬁxed parameters, and ﬁnally the coupling-entry delay. The coeﬃcient, detector, approximation and
trace estimates impose bounds in this same order. At each stage only ﬁnitely many demands of its
prescribed ﬁnite degree and derivative order occur. Their maximum is a ﬁnite demand. Increase
the stage parameters to meet it. Increasing later block lower bounds and delays preserves the earlier
requirements. Taking the increasing degree and derivative orders in this construction meets every
ﬁxed ﬁnite request eventually.
The exact one-step identities and the banked-history convergence then construct the calibrated
Wilson family, including its common insertion tokens, before any volume subsequence is speciﬁed.
Its represented action at the ﬁnest cutoﬀis the Wilson action in the theorem. Positivity of its

Conclusion

The construction connects a ﬁnite Wilson probability law to a common continuum hierarchy through
explicit kernels, nonlinear integrations, calibrated histories and physical coeﬃcient spaces. The full
mesh limit at each suitable ﬁxed period precedes the outer volume reﬁnement. Reﬂection positivity,
the phase algebra and the tested boundary construction then give the ﬁelds on their common cyclic
domain. The operator-product and contact constructions retain their ﬁnite horizons and chosen
devices on that same hierarchy.
The stress calculation returns to actual ﬁnite local functions, controls their equation residuals
and ﬁxes the centered trace amplitude. Its logarithmic short-distance asymptotic yields the ﬁnite
mass-shell and Maxwell comparison conclusions with the hypotheses stated above. No positive
mass gap is asserted.
